## Course Overview

Welcome to the Cohortia C++ Certified Professional Programmer (CPP) course, an advanced journey designed to equip you with the deep expertise required to master modern C++ development. This comprehensive program delves into the intricate features and powerful paradigms that define C++, preparing you not just for certification, but for real-world application in high-performance computing, system programming, game development, and embedded systems. We will move beyond basic syntax and object-oriented fundamentals to explore the sophisticated tools and techniques that professional C++ developers employ daily, focusing on efficiency, robustness, and maintainability.

This course is ideally suited for experienced programmers who possess a solid foundation in C++ syntax, object-oriented programming concepts, pointers, and basic memory management. If you've completed an intermediate C++ course or have equivalent practical experience and are looking to elevate your skills to an expert level, this program is for you. Aspiring software engineers, system architects, game developers, and anyone aiming for professional C++ certification will find immense value in the rigorous curriculum. Be prepared to engage with complex topics, challenging exercises, and extensive code examples that push the boundaries of your current understanding.

Throughout this course, you will learn to harness the full power of C++'s advanced features, including sophisticated template metaprogramming, the comprehensive Standard Template Library (STL), robust exception handling mechanisms, and modern concurrency primitives. We will explore how to write highly optimized, thread-safe, and memory-efficient code, crucial for applications where performance is paramount. The curriculum is structured to build your knowledge progressively, ensuring that each new concept is firmly rooted in prior learning, culminating in a holistic understanding of advanced C++ development.

By the end of this program, you won't just understand advanced C++ concepts; you'll be able to apply them effectively to solve complex programming challenges. You will gain the confidence to design and implement sophisticated software solutions, optimize performance bottlenecks, and write clean, maintainable, and scalable C++ code. This course serves as a direct pathway to achieving professional C++ certification, validating your expertise and opening doors to advanced career opportunities in technology.

Upon successful completion of this course, learners will be able to:

*   Master advanced object-oriented programming techniques, including abstract classes, pure virtual functions, and complex inheritance patterns.
*   Implement robust memory management strategies using smart pointers and custom allocators to prevent memory leaks and improve resource safety.
*   Design and utilize effective exception handling mechanisms, including RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization), to create resilient and fault-tolerant applications.
*   Develop generic and reusable code components using function templates, class templates, and advanced template metaprogramming techniques.
*   Effectively leverage the Standard Template Library (STL) containers, algorithms, and iterators for efficient data manipulation and problem-solving.
*   Implement concurrent and multi-threaded applications using C++11/14/17/20 features like `std::thread`, mutexes, condition variables, and atomics.
*   Apply modern C++ features and idioms (e.g., lambdas, move semantics, `constexpr`, `std::optional`) to write more expressive and efficient code.
*   Understand and implement common design patterns to structure complex C++ applications for scalability and maintainability.
*   Analyze and optimize the performance of C++ applications using profiling tools and best practices.
*   Prepare thoroughly for professional C++ certification exams by mastering the breadth and depth of advanced C++ topics.

# Module 1: Advanced Object-Oriented Programming

**Module Goal:** To master advanced C++ object-oriented programming techniques, including inheritance, polymorphism, abstract classes, and virtual functions, enabling the design of robust and extensible class hierarchies.

---

### Chapter 1.1 — Deep Dive into Inheritance and Access Specifiers

#### Learning objectives
*   Explain the different types of inheritance (public, protected, private) and their impact on member access.
*   Analyze how access specifiers (public, protected, private) control visibility within inheritance hierarchies.
*   Implement various inheritance scenarios, demonstrating proper use of access specifiers.
*   Identify the "diamond problem" in multiple inheritance and understand how virtual inheritance resolves it.
*   Apply best practices for designing robust and maintainable class hierarchies using inheritance.

#### Detailed lesson content
Welcome to the first chapter of our advanced C++ journey! We're diving straight into the heart of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): inheritance. You've likely encountered the basics of inheritance, where one class (the derived class) acquires properties and behaviors from another (the base class). But C++ offers a nuanced approach to inheritance, particularly through its access specifiers, which profoundly impact how derived classes and external code can interact with inherited members. Understanding these nuances is crucial for designing robust, secure, and extensible class hierarchies.

Let's begin by revisiting the three primary access specifiers: `public`, `protected`, and `private`. When a member (data or function) is declared `public` in a base class, it is accessible from anywhere: within the base class, within any derived class, and from objects of the base or derived class. `private` members, on the other hand, are strictly confined to the base class itself; they cannot be accessed directly by derived classes or external code. The `protected` specifier is where things get interesting in the context of inheritance. A `protected` member is accessible within the base class and within any derived class, but *not* from objects of the base or derived class directly through the public interface. Think of `protected` as a middle ground, allowing derived classes to have privileged access while maintaining encapsulation from the outside world.

Now, let's combine these with the *type* of inheritance. C++ allows you to inherit publicly, protectedly, or privately. This inheritance type dictates how the base class's `public` and `protected` members are treated in the *derived class's* access scope.

1.  **Public Inheritance:** This is the most common and intuitive form. When a class `Derived` publicly inherits from `Base`, the `public` members of `Base` become `public` members of `Derived`, and the `protected` members of `Base` become `protected` members of `Derived`. `private` members of `Base` remain `private` and are inaccessible to `Derived`. Public inheritance models an "is-a" relationship, meaning a `Derived` object *is a* `Base` object and should exhibit the `Base`'s public interface. For example, a `Car` *is a* `Vehicle`.

    ```cpp
    class Vehicle {
    public:
        void startEngine() { /* ... */ }
    protected:
        int fuelLevel;
    private:
        std::string chassisNumber; // Inaccessible to Car
    };

    class Car : public Vehicle {
    public:
        void drive() {
            startEngine(); // OK: Vehicle's public member
            fuelLevel = 80; // OK: Vehicle's protected member
            // chassisNumber = "XYZ"; // ERROR: Vehicle's private member
        }
    };

    int main() {
        Car myCar;
        myCar.startEngine(); // OK: Car's public member (inherited from Vehicle)
        // myCar.fuelLevel = 100; // ERROR: Car's protected member
    }
    ```

2.  **Protected Inheritance:** If `Derived` protectedly inherits from `Base`, then `public` and `protected` members of `Base` both become `protected` members of `Derived`. This means they are accessible within `Derived` and any further derived classes, but *not* through an object of `Derived` from outside. This is useful when you want to expose the base class's interface only to subsequent derived classes, not to the general public. It's a stronger form of encapsulation than public inheritance for the base's public interface.

    ```cpp
    class Device {
    public:
        void powerOn() { /* ... */ }
    protected:
        int deviceID;
    };

    class SmartDevice : protected Device { // Protected inheritance
    public:
        void connect() {
            powerOn(); // OK: Device's public member becomes protected in SmartDevice
            deviceID = 123; // OK: Device's protected member becomes protected in SmartDevice
        }
    };

    class IoTDevice : public SmartDevice { // Further derived
    public:
        void registerDevice() {
            powerOn(); // OK: SmartDevice's protected member (originally Device's public)
            deviceID = 456; // OK: SmartDevice's protected member (originally Device's protected)
        }
    };

    int main() {
        SmartDevice sd;
        // sd.powerOn(); // ERROR: powerOn() is protected in SmartDevice
        IoTDevice iotd;
        // iotd.powerOn(); // ERROR: powerOn() is protected in IoTDevice
    }
    ```

3.  **Private Inheritance:** When `Derived` privately inherits from `Base`, both `public` and `protected` members of `Base` become `private` members of `Derived`. This means they are accessible only within `Derived` itself. They are *not* accessible to any further derived classes, nor from objects of `Derived` from outside. Private inheritance typically models a "has-a" or "implemented-in-terms-of" relationship, where the derived class uses the base class's implementation details but doesn't expose its interface. It's a way to reuse code without exposing the base class's public interface. For example, a `Stack` might privately inherit from a `List` to reuse its underlying storage, but a `Stack` is not a `List` in terms of its public interface.

    ```cpp
    class Logger {
    public:
        void logMessage(const std::string& msg) { /* ... */ }
    protected:
        int logLevel;
    };

    class FileHandler : private Logger { // Private inheritance
    public:
        void writeToFile(const std::string& data) {
            logMessage("Writing data..."); // OK: Logger's public member becomes private in FileHandler
            logLevel = 2; // OK: Logger's protected member becomes private in FileHandler
            // ... actual file writing logic ...
        }
    };

    class SecureFileHandler : public FileHandler {
    public:
        void encryptAndWrite(const std::string& data) {
            // logMessage("Encrypting..."); // ERROR: logMessage() is private in FileHandler
            // logLevel = 3; // ERROR: logLevel is private in FileHandler
            writeToFile(data); // OK, calling FileHandler's own public method
        }
    };

    int main() {
        FileHandler fh;
        // fh.logMessage("Test"); // ERROR: logMessage() is private in FileHandler
    }
    ```

**Common Mistakes and Best Practices:**
A common mistake is using public inheritance when a "has-a" relationship is more appropriate. If `Derived` doesn't truly *is-a* `Base`, consider composition (where `Derived` contains an object of `Base`) instead of inheritance. This avoids exposing unnecessary interfaces and reduces coupling. For instance, a `Car` *has an* `Engine`, it doesn't *is-a* `Engine`.

Another pitfall is overusing `protected` members. While `protected` offers flexibility to derived classes, it also breaks encapsulation to some extent. Changes to `protected` members in the base class can inadvertently break derived classes, making refactoring harder. Strive to make base class members `private` by default, exposing only what's necessary through `public` or `protected` methods.

**Multiple Inheritance and the Diamond Problem:**
C++ supports multiple inheritance, where a class can inherit from more than one base class. While powerful, it introduces complexities, most notably the "diamond problem." Consider a scenario where `ClassB` and `ClassC` both inherit from `ClassA`, and then `ClassD` inherits from both `ClassB` and `ClassC`. If `ClassA` has a member variable or function, `ClassD` would inherit *two copies* of that member (one via `ClassB` and one via `ClassC`), leading to ambiguity when accessing it.

```cpp
class A {
public:
    void commonMethod() { /* ... */ }
    int value;
};

class B : public A { /* ... */ };
class C : public A { /* ... */ };

class D : public B, public C {
public:
    void accessCommon() {
        // commonMethod(); // ERROR: Ambiguous call to commonMethod()
        // value = 10; // ERROR: Ambiguous access to value
        B::commonMethod(); // OK: Explicitly call B's version
        C::value = 20;     // OK: Explicitly access C's version
    }
};
```

To resolve the diamond problem and ensure only a single instance of the common base class (`A` in this case) is inherited, C++ provides **virtual inheritance**. By declaring the inheritance from `A` as `virtual` in `B` and `C`, `D` will receive only one shared `A` subobject.

```cpp
class A {
public:
    void commonMethod() { std::cout << "A's method\n"; }
    int value;
};

class B : virtual public A { /* ... */ }; // Virtual inheritance
class C : virtual public A { /* ... */ }; // Virtual inheritance

class D : public B, public C {
public:
    void accessCommon() {
        commonMethod(); // OK: Calls the single A::commonMethod()
        value = 10;     // OK: Accesses the single A::value
    }
};

int main() {
    D objD;
    objD.commonMethod(); // Output: A's method
    objD.value = 100;
    std::cout << objD.value << std::endl; // Output: 100
}
```
Virtual inheritance comes with a slight performance overhead and specific initialization rules (the most derived class is responsible for initializing the virtual base), but it's the standard solution for the diamond problem. Use it judiciously, as multiple inheritance itself can often be refactored into composition or interface-based designs to improve clarity and reduce complexity.

In summary, mastering the various forms of inheritance and the precise control offered by access specifiers is fundamental to writing effective, maintainable, and secure C++ code. Always consider the "is-a" vs. "has-a" relationship when choosing between inheritance and composition, and be mindful of the diamond problem when venturing into multiple inheritance.

#### Key concepts
*   **Inheritance:** A mechanism where one class (derived class) acquires properties and behaviors from another class (base class).
*   **Base Class:** The class whose members are inherited.
*   **Derived Class:** The class that inherits members from a base class.
*   **Public Inheritance:** `public` members of the base become `public` in the derived; `protected` members become `protected`. Models an "is-a" relationship.
*   **Protected Inheritance:** `public` and `protected` members of the base both become `protected` in the derived. Restricts external access to base class public interface.
*   **Private Inheritance:** `public` and `protected` members of the base both become `private` in the derived. Models a "has-a" or "implemented-in-terms-of" relationship, hiding the base's interface.
*   **Access Specifiers (`public`, `protected`, `private`):** Keywords that control the visibility and accessibility of class members.
*   **Diamond Problem:** An ambiguity that arises in multiple inheritance when a class inherits from two classes that share a common base, resulting in two copies of the base class's members.
*   **Virtual Inheritance:** A C++ mechanism to resolve the diamond problem by ensuring that a common base class is inherited only once by the most derived class.

#### Hands-on activity
**Activity: Designing a Hierarchical Logging System**

**Scenario:** You need to design a logging system with different levels of access and extensibility. There's a core `Logger` class, but you want to create specialized loggers like `ConsoleLogger` and `FileLogger`, potentially with further specializations. Use different inheritance types to control access to internal logging mechanisms.

**Instructions:**
1.  Create a base class `Logger` with a `protected` member `logLevel` (an `int`) and a `public` method `log(const std::string& message)`. The `log` method should print the message along with the `logLevel`.
2.  Create `ConsoleLogger` that `publicly` inherits from `Logger`. It should have a method `displayLog(const std::string& message)` that calls the base `log` method.
3.  Create `FileLogger` that `privately` inherits from `Logger`. It should have a method `writeLogToFile(const std::string& filename, const std::string& message)`. Inside `writeLogToFile`, it should set its `logLevel` (inherited privately) and then call the base `log` method.
4.  Create `SecureFileLogger` that `publicly` inherits from `FileLogger`. Try to access `logLevel` or `log()` directly from `SecureFileLogger` and observe the compilation errors. Then, use `FileLogger`'s public interface to perform logging.

**Code Template:**

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <fstream> // For FileLogger

// 1. Base Logger class
class Logger {
protected:
    int logLevel; // Protected member
public:
    Logger(int level = 0) : logLevel(level) {}
    void log(const std::string& message) {
        std::cout << "[Level " << logLevel << "] " << message << std::endl;
    }
};

// 2. ConsoleLogger (Public Inheritance)
class ConsoleLogger : public Logger {
public:
    ConsoleLogger(int level) : Logger(level) {}
    void displayLog(const std::string& message) {
        // Call base log method
        log(message);
    }
    // Try to access logLevel directly here - it should be protected
    void testAccess() {
        // logLevel = 1; // This should compile because it's protected in ConsoleLogger
        std::cout << "ConsoleLogger can access protected logLevel: " << logLevel << std::endl;
    }
};

// 3. FileLogger (Private Inheritance)
class FileLogger : private Logger {
public:
    FileLogger(int level) : Logger(level) {}
    void writeLogToFile(const std::string& filename, const std::string& message) {
        // Set the privately inherited logLevel
        logLevel = 5; // This should compile because it's private in FileLogger
        std::ofstream file(filename, std::ios_base::app);
        if (file.is_open()) {
            // Call the privately inherited log method
            // log(message); // This will call the base log method, which prints to console for this example
            file << "[File Log Level " << logLevel << "] " << message << std::endl;
            file.close();
            std::cout << "Logged to file: " << filename << std::endl;
        } else {
            std::cerr << "Error opening file: " << filename << std::endl;
        }
    }
    // Add a public method to demonstrate that FileLogger can still use base methods internally
    void internalLog(const std::string& message) {
        log(message); // OK, accessible within FileLogger
    }
};

// 4. SecureFileLogger (Public Inheritance from FileLogger)
class SecureFileLogger : public FileLogger {
public:
    SecureFileLogger(int level) : FileLogger(level) {}
    void encryptAndWrite(const std::string& filename, const std::string& message) {
        std::cout << "Encrypting message before writing..." << std::endl;
        // Try to access logLevel or log() directly from base Logger via FileLogger
        // logLevel = 10; // ERROR: logLevel is private in FileLogger
        // log("Attempting to log from SecureFileLogger directly"); // ERROR: log() is private in FileLogger

        // Must use FileLogger's public interface
        writeLogToFile(filename, "[ENCRYPTED] " + message);
    }
};

int main() {
    ConsoleLogger cl(1);
    cl.displayLog("This is a console message.");
    cl.testAccess();
    // cl.logLevel = 2; // ERROR: logLevel is protected in ConsoleLogger, inaccessible from main

    FileLogger fl(3);
    fl.writeLogToFile("app.log", "This is a file message.");
    fl.internalLog("This message also goes to console from FileLogger's internal method.");
    // fl.log("Direct access to FileLogger's base log method."); // ERROR: log() is private in FileLogger

    SecureFileLogger sfl(4);
    sfl.encryptAndWrite("secure_app.log", "Sensitive data here.");
    // sfl.writeLogToFile("another.log", "Another message."); // OK, calling FileLogger's public method

    return 0;
}
```

#### Assessment idea
1.  **Question:** Consider the following C++ classes:
    ```cpp
    class Base {
    public:
        void publicMethod() { /* ... */ }
    protected:
        void protectedMethod() { /* ... */ }
    private:
        void privateMethod() { /* ... */ }
    };

    class DerivedA : public Base {
        // ...
    };

    class DerivedB : protected Base {
        // ...
    };

    class DerivedC : private Base {
        // ...
    };
    ```
    Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding member access from an object of `DerivedB` (e.g., `DerivedB objB;`) and from an object of `DerivedC` (e.g., `DerivedC objC;`) in `main()`?
    A) `objB.publicMethod()` is accessible, and `objC.publicMethod()` is accessible.
    B) `objB.publicMethod()` is accessible, and `objC.publicMethod()` is NOT accessible.
    C) `objB.publicMethod()` is NOT accessible, and `objC.publicMethod()` is accessible.
    D) `objB.publicMethod()` is NOT accessible, and `objC.publicMethod()` is NOT accessible.

    **Correct Answer:** D) `objB.publicMethod()` is NOT accessible, and `objC.publicMethod()` is NOT accessible.

    **Explanation:**
    *   For `DerivedB : protected Base`: When `Base` is inherited `protectedly`, its `public` and `protected` members become `protected` in `DerivedB`. Therefore, `publicMethod()` becomes `protected` in `DerivedB` and cannot be accessed from an `objB` instance in `main()`.
    *   For `DerivedC : private Base`: When `Base` is inherited `privately`, its `public` and `protected` members become `private` in `DerivedC`. Therefore, `publicMethod()` becomes `private` in `DerivedC` and cannot be accessed from an `objC` instance in `main()`.

2.  **Question:** You are designing a system where a `Manager` class needs to aggregate `Employee` objects and manage them. The `Employee` class has a `protected` method `calculatePayroll()` that should only be accessible by the `Manager` or other internal HR-related classes, but not by external code. Which inheritance type should `Manager` use if it were to inherit from `Employee` to achieve this, and why might composition be a better alternative?

    **Correct Answer:** If `Manager` were to inherit from `Employee`, **protected inheritance** would be the most suitable type.

    **Explanation:**
    *   **Protected Inheritance:** If `Manager : protected Employee`, then `Employee`'s `public` and `protected` members (like `calculatePayroll()`) would become `protected` in `Manager`. This means `Manager` could call `calculatePayroll()` internally, and any classes further derived from `Manager` could also access it. However, an external `Manager` object (e.g., `Manager m; m.calculatePayroll();`) would *not* be able to call it, satisfying the requirement.
    *   **Why Composition is Better:** While protected inheritance technically fulfills the access requirement, it implies an "is-a" relationship (`Manager` *is an* `Employee`), which is semantically incorrect in most real-world scenarios. A `Manager` *manages* `Employee`s; it is not an `Employee` itself in the same hierarchical sense. **Composition** (where `Manager` *has a* list or vector of `Employee` objects) is a much more appropriate design. The `Manager` class would then interact with `Employee` objects through their public interfaces, or if `calculatePayroll()` needs to be called, it would be a public method of `Employee` that `Manager` calls on its contained `Employee` objects, or `Manager` itself would have a method that takes an `Employee` and performs the calculation. This avoids misrepresenting the relationship and generally leads to more flexible and less coupled designs.

### Chapter 1.2 — Abstract Classes and Pure Virtual Functions: Defining Contracts

#### Learning objectives
*   Understand the purpose and syntax of pure virtual functions in C++.
*   Define and identify abstract classes, recognizing their instantiation restrictions.
*   Explain how abstract classes enforce an interface contract for derived classes.
*   Implement concrete derived classes that correctly fulfill the abstract class's contract.
*   Identify common pitfalls when working with abstract classes and pure virtual functions.

#### Detailed lesson content
Welcome back, aspiring C++ professionals! In our journey through advanced object-oriented programming, we've already explored the power of inheritance and basic polymorphism using virtual functions. We saw how a base class pointer or reference can invoke the correct overridden method in a derived class at runtime. But what if a base class doesn't have a meaningful default implementation for a particular virtual function? Or, more importantly, what if we *want* to ensure that *every* derived class *must* provide its own specific implementation for a certain behavior? This is where abstract classes and pure virtual functions come into play, allowing us to define a contract that derived classes must adhere to.

Imagine you're designing a graphics application. You might have a base class called `Shape`. Every `Shape` should logically have an `area()` and a `draw()` method. However, what is the "area" of a generic `Shape`? How do you "draw" a generic `Shape`? These concepts are too abstract to implement meaningfully in the `Shape` base class itself. The actual calculation of area and the drawing mechanism depend entirely on the specific type of shape (e.g., `Circle`, `Rectangle`, `Triangle`). This is a perfect scenario for pure virtual functions.

A **pure virtual function** is a virtual function declared in a base class that has no definition in the base class and is initialized with `= 0`. The syntax looks like this: `virtual void draw() = 0;`. The `= 0` part is not assigning zero to anything; it's a special C++ syntax indicating that this function is pure virtual. When a class contains at least one pure virtual function, it becomes an **abstract class**.

The crucial consequence of an abstract class is that you **cannot instantiate it directly**. You cannot create an object of an abstract class type. For example, if `Shape` is an abstract class, `Shape myShape;` would result in a compilation error. This makes perfect sense: how could you create a generic `Shape` object if it doesn't even know how to draw itself or calculate its area? Abstract classes serve as blueprints or interfaces; they define a common set of behaviors that all derived classes *must* implement. They enforce a contract.

To make an abstract class usable, you must derive a concrete class from it and provide implementations for *all* its pure virtual functions. If a derived class fails to implement even one pure virtual function from its base abstract class, that derived class itself becomes abstract, and you still cannot instantiate it. This chain continues until a derived class provides implementations for *all* inherited pure virtual functions, at which point it becomes a concrete class that *can* be instantiated.

Let's illustrate with our `Shape` example:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <cmath> // For M_PI

// Base abstract class
class Shape {
public:
    // Pure virtual function for calculating area
    virtual double area() const = 0; 
    // Pure virtual function for drawing
    virtual void draw() const = 0; 

    // A non-pure virtual function can still exist
    virtual std::string getName() const {
        return "Generic Shape";
    }

    // A concrete function can also exist
    void printInfo() const {
        std::cout << "Shape Name: " << getName() << std::endl;
        // This will call the derived class's area()
        std::cout << "Area: " << area() << std::endl; 
    }

    // Virtual destructor is crucial for polymorphic deletion
    virtual ~Shape() {
        std::cout << "Shape destructor called." << std::endl;
    }
};

// Concrete derived class: Circle
class Circle : public Shape {
private:
    double radius;
public:
    Circle(double r) : radius(r) {}

    // Must implement area()
    double area() const override {
        return M_PI * radius * radius;
    }

    // Must implement draw()
    void draw() const override {
        std::cout << "Drawing a Circle with radius " << radius << std::endl;
    }

    std::string getName() const override {
        return "Circle";
    }

    ~Circle() {
        std::cout << "Circle destructor called." << std::endl;
    }
};

// Concrete derived class: Rectangle
class Rectangle : public Shape {
private:
    double width;
    double height;
public:
    Rectangle(double w, double h) : width(w), height(h) {}

    // Must implement area()
    double area() const override {
        return width * height;
    }

    // Must implement draw()
    void draw() const override {
        std::cout << "Drawing a Rectangle with width " << width << " and height " << height << std::endl;
    }

    std::string getName() const override {
        return "Rectangle";
    }

    ~Rectangle() {
        std::cout << "Rectangle destructor called." << std::endl;
    }
};

// Example of a class that is still abstract because it doesn't implement all pure virtual functions
class IncompleteShape : public Shape {
public:
    double area() const override {
        return 0.0; // Implemented area, but not draw()
    }
    // Still abstract because draw() is not implemented
};

int main() {
    // Shape s; // ERROR: Cannot instantiate abstract class

    Circle c(5.0);
    Rectangle r(4.0, 6.0);

    c.printInfo(); // Uses Shape's printInfo, which calls Circle's area()
    c.draw();

    r.printInfo();
    r.draw();

    std::cout << "\n--- Using polymorphism with a vector of Shape pointers ---\n";
    std::vector<Shape*> shapes;
    shapes.push_back(new Circle(3.0));
    shapes.push_back(new Rectangle(2.0, 7.0));

    for (const auto& shape_ptr : shapes) {
        shape_ptr->printInfo();
        shape_ptr->draw();
        std::cout << std::endl;
    }

    // Clean up dynamically allocated memory
    for (const auto& shape_ptr : shapes) {
        delete shape_ptr;
    }

    // IncompleteShape is abstract, cannot be instantiated
    // IncompleteShape is; // ERROR: Cannot instantiate abstract class

    return 0;
}
```

In this example, `Shape` is an abstract class because `area()` and `draw()` are pure virtual. `Circle` and `Rectangle` are concrete classes because they provide implementations for both `area()` and `draw()`. Notice how `printInfo()` in the `Shape` base class can still call `area()`, relying on the dynamic dispatch mechanism (polymorphism) to invoke the correct `area()` implementation from the derived class at runtime. This is a powerful demonstration of how abstract classes define an interface that can be partially implemented or fully utilized by base class methods, even if the specific implementation details are left to derived classes.

A common mistake is forgetting to declare a virtual destructor in your base class, especially when dealing with polymorphic hierarchies where objects are deleted via base class pointers. If `Shape` did not have a virtual destructor, `delete shape_ptr;` in `main` might only call the `Shape` destructor, leading to a memory leak if `Circle` or `Rectangle` had specific cleanup logic in their destructors. Always remember: if a class has any virtual functions, it should almost certainly have a virtual destructor.

Another common pitfall is trying to instantiate an abstract class directly. The compiler will catch this, but understanding *why* it's forbidden is key. It's because the class is incomplete; it has declared functions that it cannot fulfill itself. Similarly, if a derived class fails to implement *all* pure virtual functions, it also becomes abstract. This can sometimes be a subtle bug if you intend for a class to be concrete but forget an implementation.

In summary, abstract classes and pure virtual functions are fundamental tools for designing robust and extensible class hierarchies in C++. They allow you to define clear contracts for derived classes, ensuring that specific behaviors are implemented while maintaining the flexibility of polymorphism. They are the backbone of many design patterns, particularly those that rely on defining an interface.

#### Key concepts
*   **Pure Virtual Function:** A virtual function declared in a base class that has no definition and is initialized with `= 0`. Syntax: `virtual ReturnType functionName(parameters) = 0;`.
*   **Abstract Class:** A class that contains at least one pure virtual function.
*   **Instantiation Restriction:** Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly; you cannot create objects of an abstract class type.
*   **Interface Contract:** Abstract classes define a contract, forcing derived classes to provide implementations for all pure virtual functions.
*   **Concrete Class:** A class that is not abstract, meaning it has no pure virtual functions (either it never declared any, or it has implemented all pure virtual functions inherited from its base classes).
*   **Virtual Destructor:** A destructor declared as `virtual` in a base class, essential for correctly deallocating memory in polymorphic hierarchies to ensure derived class destructors are called.

#### Hands-on activity
**Challenge: Building a Payment Processor Hierarchy**

You need to design a system for processing different types of payments. All payment methods should have a way to `processPayment()` and `getPaymentDetails()`. However, the exact implementation of these methods varies significantly between credit card, PayPal, and cryptocurrency payments.

1.  **Create an abstract base class `PaymentMethod`:**
    *   It should have a pure virtual function `virtual bool processPayment(double amount) = 0;`
    *   It should have a pure virtual function `virtual std::string getPaymentDetails() const = 0;`
    *   Include a virtual destructor.
    *   Add a concrete member function `void displayPaymentStatus(double amount) const;` that uses `getPaymentDetails()` and prints a generic message.

2.  **Create concrete derived classes:**
    *   `CreditCardPayment`: Stores card number, expiry, CVV. Implement `processPayment` (simulate success/failure based on amount or card number) and `getPaymentDetails`.
    *   `PayPalPayment`: Stores email. Implement `processPayment` (simulate success/failure) and `getPaymentDetails`.
    *   `CryptoPayment`: Stores wallet address, currency type. Implement `processPayment` (simulate success/failure) and `getPaymentDetails`.

3.  **Demonstrate polymorphism:**
    *   In `main()`, create a `std::vector<PaymentMethod*>` and add instances of `CreditCardPayment`, `PayPalPayment`, and `CryptoPayment`.
    *   Iterate through the vector, call `processPayment()` with different amounts, and then `displayPaymentStatus()` for each.
    *   Remember to clean up memory using `delete`.

**Starter Code Template:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <numeric> // For std::accumulate (optional)

// 1. Create an abstract base class PaymentMethod
class PaymentMethod {
public:
    virtual bool processPayment(double amount) = 0;
    virtual std::string getPaymentDetails() const = 0;
    
    virtual void displayPaymentStatus(double amount) const {
        std::cout << "Attempting to process " << amount << " using " << getPaymentDetails() << std::endl;
        // In a real scenario, you'd check the return of processPayment here
    }

    virtual ~PaymentMethod() {
        std::cout << "PaymentMethod destructor called." << std::endl;
    }
};

// 2. Create concrete derived classes: CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, CryptoPayment
//    Implement their constructors, processPayment(), and getPaymentDetails()

// Example: CreditCardPayment
class CreditCardPayment : public PaymentMethod {
private:
    std::string cardNumber;
    std::string expiryDate;
    std::string cvv;
public:
    CreditCardPayment(const std::string& cardNum, const std::string& expiry, const std::string& c)
        : cardNumber(cardNum), expiryDate(expiry), cvv(c) {}

    bool processPayment(double amount) override {
        std::cout << "Processing credit card payment for " << amount << "..." << std::endl;
        // Simulate payment logic: success if amount < 1000, failure otherwise
        if (amount < 1000.0) {
            std::cout << "Credit card payment successful." << std::endl;
            return true;
        } else {
            std::cout << "Credit card payment failed: amount too high." << std::endl;
            return false;
        }
    }

    std::string getPaymentDetails() const override {
        // Mask card number for security
        return "Credit Card (**** " + cardNumber.substr(cardNumber.length() - 4) + ", Exp: " + expiryDate + ")";
    }

    ~CreditCardPayment() {
        std::cout << "CreditCardPayment destructor called." << std::endl;
    }
};

// TODO: Implement PayPalPayment and CryptoPayment similarly

int main() {
    // 3. Demonstrate polymorphism
    std::vector<PaymentMethod*> payments;

    payments.push_back(new CreditCardPayment("1234-5678-9012-3456", "12/25", "123"));
    // payments.push_back(new PayPalPayment("user@example.com")); // Uncomment after implementing
    // payments.push_back(new CryptoPayment("0xAbc...123", "BTC")); // Uncomment after implementing

    std::cout << "--- Processing Payments ---\n";
    payments[0]->displayPaymentStatus(50.0);
    payments[0]->processPayment(50.0);
    std::cout << std::endl;

    payments[0]->displayPaymentStatus(1500.0);
    payments[0]->processPayment(1500.0);
    std::cout << std::endl;

    // TODO: Add more payment processing for other types once implemented

    // Clean up memory
    for (PaymentMethod* pm : payments) {
        delete pm;
    }

    return 0;
}
```

#### Assessment idea
1.  **Question:** Consider the following C++ code snippet:
    ```cpp
    class Base {
    public:
        virtual void func1() = 0;
        virtual void func2() { /* implementation */ }
        void func3() { /* implementation */ }
    };

    class DerivedA : public Base {
    public:
        void func1() override { /* DerivedA implementation */ }
        // Missing func2() override
    };

    class DerivedB : public Base {
    public:
        void func1() override { /* DerivedB implementation */ }
        void func2() override { /* DerivedB implementation */ }
    };

    int main() {
        // Line 1
        Base* b_ptr;
        // Line 2
        DerivedA objA;
        // Line 3
        DerivedB objB;
        // Line 4
        DerivedA* da_ptr = new DerivedA();
        // Line 5
        DerivedB* db_ptr = new DerivedB();
        return 0;
    }
    ```
    Which lines of code, if uncommented, would cause a compilation error, and why?

    **Answer:**
    *   **Line 1 (`Base* b_ptr;`):** This line declares a pointer to `Base`, which is perfectly fine. Pointers to abstract classes can be declared and used to point to concrete derived class objects. It does not attempt to instantiate `Base`.
    *   **Line 2 (`DerivedA objA;`):** This line would cause a compilation error. `DerivedA` inherits from `Base`, which has two pure virtual functions: `func1()` and `func2()`. While `DerivedA` implements `func1()`, it *fails to implement `func2()`*. Therefore, `DerivedA` remains an abstract class, and you cannot instantiate an object of an abstract class type.
    *   **Line 3 (`DerivedB objB;`):** This line is perfectly valid. `DerivedB` implements both `func1()` and `func2()`, making it a concrete class that can be instantiated.
    *   **Line 4 (`DerivedA* da_ptr = new DerivedA();`):** This line would cause a compilation error for the same reason as Line 2. You cannot dynamically allocate an object of an abstract class type.
    *   **Line 5 (`DerivedB* db_ptr = new DerivedB();`):** This line is valid. `DerivedB` is a concrete class and can be dynamically allocated.

    **Summary of errors:** Lines 2 and 4 would cause compilation errors because `DerivedA` is an abstract class (it doesn't implement all pure virtual functions inherited from `Base`), and abstract classes cannot be instantiated.

2.  **Question:** Explain the primary benefit of using an abstract class with pure virtual functions in a large software project. Provide a real-world analogy.

    **Answer:**
    The primary benefit of using an abstract class with pure virtual functions in a large software project is to **enforce a consistent interface or contract** across a hierarchy of related classes. It dictates that any concrete class deriving from the abstract base class *must* provide implementations for specific behaviors, without the base class needing to know or care about the exact details of those implementations. This promotes design consistency, reduces errors, and makes the system more maintainable and extensible.

    **Real-world analogy:** Think of an abstract class `Vehicle` with pure virtual functions like `startEngine()`, `accelerate()`, and `brake()`. A car manufacturer might define this `Vehicle` blueprint. They don't know *how* a specific car model (e.g., `ElectricCar`, `GasolineCar`, `HybridCar`) will implement `startEngine()` (e.g., push button, turn key, activate electric motor), but they *insist* that every vehicle they produce *must* have a way to start its engine, accelerate, and brake. The `Vehicle` abstract class defines the common "what" (what actions a vehicle can perform), while the derived concrete classes define the specific "how" (how each type of vehicle performs those actions). This ensures that any `Vehicle` object, regardless of its specific type, can be operated using the same set of commands, making the overall system predictable and manageable.

### Chapter 1.3 — Interfaces and Multiple Inheritance: Combining Behaviors

#### Learning objectives
*   Understand the concept of an "interface" in C++ and how it's implemented using abstract classes.
*   Explain the purpose and syntax of multiple inheritance in C++.
*   Identify the "diamond problem" associated with multiple inheritance.
*   Describe and apply virtual inheritance as a solution to the diamond problem.
*   Analyze the trade-offs and best practices for using multiple inheritance versus composition.

#### Detailed lesson content
Building upon our understanding of abstract classes, we can now explore how C++ allows us to define even more flexible and powerful contracts. In many object-oriented languages, an "interface" is a distinct language construct that defines a set of methods that a class must implement, without providing any implementation details or data members. C++ doesn't have a keyword `interface` like Java or C#, but we can achieve the same concept using abstract classes. An **interface in C++** is typically an abstract class that contains *only* pure virtual functions and *no* data members (or very minimal, static data). Its sole purpose is to define a contract for behavior.

Consider a scenario where you want different objects to be able to "log" messages or "serialize" themselves. You can define interfaces like `ILoggable` or `ISerializable`. The `I` prefix is a common convention to denote an interface.

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

// C++ Interface: IPrintable
// An abstract class with only pure virtual functions and no data members
class IPrintable {
public:
    virtual void print() const = 0;
    virtual ~IPrintable() = default; // Virtual destructor is good practice for interfaces
};

// C++ Interface: ISavable
class ISavable {
public:
    virtual void saveToFile(const std::string& filename) const = 0;
    virtual ~ISavable() = default;
};

// A concrete class that implements both interfaces
class Document : public IPrintable, public ISavable {
private:
    std::string content;
    std::string title;
public:
    Document(const std::string& t, const std::string& c) : title(t), content(c) {}

    void print() const override {
        std::cout << "Printing Document: " << title << "\nContent:\n" << content << std::endl;
    }

    void saveToFile(const std::string& filename) const override {
        std::cout << "Saving Document '" << title << "' to " << filename << ". Content: " << content.substr(0, 20) << "..." << std::endl;
        // In a real application, you'd write to an actual file.
    }

    std::string getTitle() const { return title; }
};

void processPrintable(const IPrintable& p) {
    std::cout << "\n--- Processing a printable item ---\n";
    p.print();
}

void processSavable(const ISavable& s, const std::string& filename) {
    std::cout << "\n--- Processing a savable item ---\n";
    s.saveToFile(filename);
}

int main() {
    Document doc("My Report", "This is the detailed content of my report. It contains important information.");

    doc.print();
    doc.saveToFile("report.txt");

    // We can use base interface pointers/references for polymorphic behavior
    processPrintable(doc);
    processSavable(doc, "another_report.txt");

    // Using a vector of interface pointers
    std::vector<IPrintable*> printables;
    printables.push_back(new Document("Letter", "Dear Sir/Madam..."));
    // Add other printable objects here

    for (const auto& p : printables) {
        p->print();
    }

    for (const auto& p : printables) {
        delete p;
    }

    return 0;
}
```
In the `Document` class, we see an example of **multiple inheritance**, where a class derives from more than one base class. The syntax is straightforward: `class Derived : public Base1, public Base2 { ... };`. Multiple inheritance allows a derived class to inherit features (both data and methods) from multiple, distinct base classes, effectively combining their functionalities. This can be incredibly powerful for modeling complex real-world relationships where an object naturally possesses characteristics and behaviors from several categories. For instance, a `FlyingCar` might inherit from both `Car` and `Aircraft`.

However, multiple inheritance in C++ comes with a significant challenge known as the **diamond problem** (or diamond of death). This occurs when a class `D` inherits from two classes, `B1` and `B2`, which both inherit from a common base class `A`. In this scenario, `D` would inherit two separate sub-objects of `A`, one through `B1` and one through `B2`. This leads to ambiguity: if `A` has a member, which `A` sub-object's member should `D` use?

Let's visualize the diamond problem:
```
      A
     / \
    B1 B2
     \ /
      D
```

If `A` has a member variable `int value;` and a method `void printValue();`, then `D` would have two `value` members and two `printValue` methods. Accessing `d.value` or `d.printValue()` would be ambiguous. The compiler would report an error, forcing you to explicitly qualify which `A` sub-object you mean (e.g., `d.B1::value`). While this resolves the ambiguity, it doesn't solve the problem of having duplicate `A` sub-objects, which can be inefficient and conceptually incorrect if `D` should only have *one* `A` part.

C++ provides a solution to the diamond problem: **virtual inheritance**. When a base class is inherited virtually, it means that only one sub-object of that base class will exist in the most derived class, even if it's inherited multiple times through different paths. You declare virtual inheritance using the `virtual` keyword in the inheritance list: `class B1 : virtual public A { ... };` and `class B2 : virtual public A { ... };`.

Let's see an example of the diamond problem and its resolution:

```cpp
// Diamond Problem Example
class Animal {
public:
    Animal() { std::cout << "Animal constructor\n"; }
    void eat() { std::cout << "Animal eats.\n"; }
    virtual ~Animal() { std::cout << "Animal destructor\n"; }
};

class Mammal : public Animal {
public:
    Mammal() { std::cout << "Mammal constructor\n"; }
    void breathe() { std::cout << "Mammal breathes.\n"; }
    virtual ~Mammal() { std::cout << "Mammal destructor\n"; }
};

class Bird : public Animal {
public:
    Bird() { std::cout << "Bird constructor\n"; }
    void fly() { std::cout << "Bird flies.\n"; }
    virtual ~Bird() { std::cout << "Bird destructor\n"; }
};

// Platypus inherits from Mammal and Bird, both of which inherit from Animal
class Platypus : public Mammal, public Bird {
public:
    Platypus() { std::cout << "Platypus constructor\n"; }
    void layEggs() { std::cout << "Platypus lays eggs.\n"; }
    virtual ~Platypus() { std::cout << "Platypus destructor\n"; }
};

// int main() {
//     Platypus p;
//     p.eat(); // ERROR: Request for member 'eat' is ambiguous
//     // To resolve manually: p.Mammal::eat(); or p.Bird::eat();
// }
```
The `p.eat()` call is ambiguous because `Platypus` inherits two `Animal` sub-objects, each with its own `eat()` method.

Now, let's solve it with virtual inheritance:

```cpp
// Diamond Problem Solution with Virtual Inheritance
class VAnimal {
public:
    VAnimal() { std::cout << "VAnimal constructor\n"; }
    void eat() { std::cout << "VAnimal eats.\n"; }
    virtual ~VAnimal() { std::cout << "VAnimal destructor\n"; }
};

class VMammal : virtual public VAnimal { // Virtual inheritance
public:
    VMammal() { std::cout << "VMammal constructor\n"; }
    void breathe() { std::cout << "VMammal breathes.\n"; }
    virtual ~VMammal() { std::cout << "VMammal destructor\n"; }
};

class VBird : virtual public VAnimal { // Virtual inheritance
public:
    VBird() { std::cout << "VBird constructor\n"; }
    void fly() { std::cout << "VBird flies.\n"; }
    virtual ~VBird() { std::cout << "VBird destructor\n"; }
};

class VPlatypus : public VMammal, public VBird {
public:
    VPlatypus() { std::cout << "VPlatypus constructor\n"; }
    void layEggs() { std::cout << "VPlatypus lays eggs.\n"; }
    virtual ~VPlatypus() { std::cout << "VPlatypus destructor\n"; }
};

int main() {
    std::cout << "--- Without Virtual Inheritance (commented out due to ambiguity) ---\n";
    // Platypus p;
    // p.eat(); // Would be ambiguous

    std::cout << "\n--- With Virtual Inheritance ---\n";
    VPlatypus vp;
    vp.eat(); // Now unambiguous!
    vp.breathe();
    vp.fly();
    vp.layEggs();

    // Observe constructor call order:
    // VAnimal constructor (called by VPlatypus directly)
    // VMammal constructor
    // VBird constructor
    // VPlatypus constructor

    // Common mistake: forgetting to initialize the virtually inherited base class
    // The most derived class (VPlatypus) is responsible for constructing the VAnimal sub-object.
    // If VPlatypus doesn't explicitly call VAnimal's constructor, VAnimal's default constructor is called.
    // If VAnimal only has a non-default constructor, VPlatypus *must* call it.
    // E.g., if VAnimal(int id) exists, VPlatypus() : VAnimal(123), VMammal(), VBird() {}
    return 0;
}
```
With virtual inheritance, `VPlatypus` now contains only one `VAnimal` sub-object, and calls to `eat()` are unambiguous. A critical point with virtual inheritance is that the **most derived class** (e.g., `VPlatypus`) is responsible for constructing the virtually inherited base class (`VAnimal`). Intermediate classes (`VMammal`, `VBird`) do not construct `VAnimal` directly; their constructors are still called, but `VAnimal`'s constructor is invoked only once by `VPlatypus`.

While multiple inheritance can be useful, especially with interfaces, it often adds complexity. A common best practice in C++ is to favor **composition over inheritance** where appropriate. Composition means a class contains objects of other classes as members, rather than inheriting from them. This creates a "has-a" relationship instead of an "is-a" relationship. For example, instead of a `Car` inheriting `Engine` and `Wheels`, a `Car` *has-a* `Engine` and *has-a* `Wheels`. Composition generally leads to more flexible designs, as you can change the components at runtime, and avoids the complexities of multiple inheritance like the diamond problem. However, for true "is-a" relationships where an object genuinely *is* multiple things (like `Document` *is* `IPrintable` and *is* `ISavable`), multiple inheritance with interfaces can be a clean and powerful solution.

Common mistakes include:
1.  **Ambiguity:** Forgetting to resolve ambiguous calls when not using virtual inheritance.
2.  **Constructor Call Order:** Misunderstanding that the most derived class is responsible for constructing the virtually inherited base class.
3.  **Overuse:** Applying multiple inheritance when composition would be a simpler and more flexible solution. It's best reserved for situations where a class genuinely needs to inherit distinct *interfaces* or orthogonal functionalities.

#### Key concepts
*   **C++ Interface:** An abstract class that contains *only* pure virtual functions and no data members, serving as a contract for behavior.
*   **Multiple Inheritance:** A feature where a class can inherit from more than one base class, combining their functionalities.
*   **Diamond Problem:** An ambiguity issue in multiple inheritance where a class inherits from two classes that share a common base, leading to duplicate sub-objects of the common base.
*   **Virtual Inheritance:** A mechanism in C++ (`virtual public Base`) used to resolve the diamond problem by ensuring that only one sub-object of a virtually inherited base class exists in the most derived class.
*   **Most Derived Class:** In virtual inheritance, the class at the bottom of the hierarchy that is responsible for constructing the virtually inherited base class.
*   **Composition over Inheritance:** A design principle that favors creating "has-a" relationships (where a class contains objects of other classes) over "is-a" relationships (inheritance) to achieve greater flexibility and avoid inheritance complexities.

**Challenge: Designing a Smart Device System**

You are tasked with designing a system for various smart devices. Some devices are `Connectable` (can connect to a network), some are `Controllable` (can be turned on/off), and some are both.

1.  **Define Interfaces:**
    *   Create an interface `IConnectable` with a pure virtual function `virtual void connect(const std::string& networkName) = 0;` and `virtual bool isConnected() const = 0;`.
    *   Create an interface `IControllable` with pure virtual functions `virtual void turnOn() = 0;` and `virtual void turnOff() = 0;` and `virtual bool isOn() const = 0;`.
    *   Remember virtual destructors for interfaces.

2.  **Implement Concrete Devices:**
    *   `SmartLight`: Inherits `IControllable`. Implement its methods.
    *   `SmartSpeaker`: Inherits `IConnectable` and `IControllable`. Implement all methods.

3.  **Demonstrate Usage:**

**Starter Code Template:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <numeric>

// 1. Define Interfaces

public:

    virtual bool isConnected() const = 0;
    virtual ~IConnectable() = default;
};

class IControllable {
public:
    virtual void turnOn() = 0;
    virtual void turnOff() = 0;
    virtual bool isOn() const = 0;
    virtual ~IControllable() = default;
};

// 2. Implement Concrete Devices
class SmartLight : public IControllable {
private:
    bool poweredOn = false;
public:
    void turnOn() override {
        poweredOn = true;
        std::cout << "SmartLight is ON." << std::endl;
    }
    void turnOff() override {
        poweredOn = false;
        std::cout << "SmartLight is OFF." << std::endl;
    }
    bool isOn() const override {
        return poweredOn;
    }
    ~SmartLight() { std::cout << "SmartLight destructor called.\n"; }
};

// TODO: Implement SmartSpeaker (inherits IConnectable, IControllable)
class SmartSpeaker : public IConnectable, public IControllable {
private:
    std::string currentNetwork;
    bool connected = false;
    bool poweredOn = false;
public:

        connected = true;

// TODO: Implement SmartSensor (inherits IConnectable)
class SmartSensor : public IConnectable {

int main() {
    std::cout << "--- Smart Device System Demo ---\n";

    SmartLight light;
    light.turnOn();
    std::cout << "Light is " << (light.isOn() ? "on" : "off") << std::endl;
    light.turnOff();

    speaker.connect("MyHomeWiFi");
    speaker.turnOn();

    std::vector<IConnectable*> connectableDevices;

    connectableDevices.push_back(new SmartSensor());  // Add a new sensor for vector demo

    for (IConnectable* device : connectableDevices) {

    }
```

#### Assessment idea
1.  **Question:** Explain the "diamond problem" in C++ multiple inheritance. Provide a simple class hierarchy (A, B1, B2, D) to illustrate it, and then show how `virtual` inheritance resolves the issue.

    **Answer:**
    The **diamond problem** occurs in C++ multiple inheritance when a class `D` inherits from two classes, `B1` and `B2`, which themselves both inherit from a common base class `A`. This creates a "diamond" shape in the inheritance hierarchy. The problem arises because `D` ends up with two separate sub-objects of `A` (one inherited via `B1` and another via `B2`). If `A` has any member variables or functions, accessing them through an object of type `D` becomes ambiguous because the compiler doesn't know which `A` sub-object's member to use.

    **Illustration of the problem:**
    ```cpp
    class A {
    public:
        int value = 10;
        void printValue() { std::cout << "Value: " << value << std::endl; }
    };

    class B1 : public A {};
    class B2 : public A {};

    class D : public B1, public B2 {};

    // int main() {
    //     D d_obj;
    //     d_obj.printValue(); // ERROR: Request for member 'printValue' is ambiguous
    //     std::cout << d_obj.value; // ERROR: Request for member 'value' is ambiguous
    // }
    ```
    In this example, `d_obj` has two `A::value` members and two `A::printValue()` methods, leading to ambiguity.

    **Resolution with `virtual` inheritance:**
    To resolve the diamond problem, we use `virtual` inheritance for the common base class (`A`) in the intermediate classes (`B1` and `B2`). This ensures that only a single sub-object of `A` is created in the most derived class (`D`).

    ```cpp
    class A_Virtual {
    public:
        int value = 10;
        void printValue() { std::cout << "Virtual Value: " << value << std::endl; }
    };

    class B1_Virtual : virtual public A_Virtual {}; // Notice 'virtual'
    class B2_Virtual : virtual public A_Virtual {}; // Notice 'virtual'

    class D_Resolved : public B1_Virtual, public B2_Virtual {};

    int main() {
        D_Resolved d_resolved_obj;
        d_resolved_obj.printValue(); // OK: Now unambiguous, prints "Virtual Value: 10"
        std::cout << "Accessing value: " << d_resolved_obj.value << std::endl; // OK
        return 0;
    }
    ```
    With `virtual public A_Virtual`, `D_Resolved` contains only one `A_Virtual` sub-object, making all accesses unambiguous. The most derived class (`D_Resolved`) is responsible for constructing the `A_Virtual` base.

2.  **Question:** You are designing a system for managing various types of media files. You need to ensure that all media files can be `play()`ed and `getMetadata()` retrieved. Some media files might also be `editable()`. How would you design this using C++ interfaces and multiple inheritance, if applicable? Provide a minimal code sketch.

    **Answer:**
    We would design this system using C++ interfaces (abstract classes with pure virtual functions) to define the contracts for `Playable`, `MetadataProvider`, and `Editable` behaviors. Multiple inheritance would be used for media types that exhibit more than one of these behaviors.

    **Code Sketch:**
    ```cpp
    #include <iostream>
    #include <string>
    #include <map>

    // Interface for Playable media
    class IPlayable {
    public:
        virtual void play() = 0;
        virtual ~IPlayable() = default;
    };

    // Interface for Metadata Provider
    class IMetadataProvider {
    public:
        virtual std::map<std::string, std::string> getMetadata() const = 0;
        virtual ~IMetadataProvider() = default;
    };

    // Interface for Editable media
    class IEditable {
    public:
        virtual void edit(const std::string& newContent) = 0;
        virtual ~IEditable() = default;
    };

    // Concrete class: AudioFile (Playable, MetadataProvider)
    class AudioFile : public IPlayable, public IMetadataProvider {
    private:
        std::string title;
        std::string artist;
        std::string audioData;
    public:
        AudioFile(const std::string& t, const std::string& a, const std::string& data)
            : title(t), artist(a), audioData(data) {}

        void play() override {
            std::cout << "Playing audio: " << title << " by " << artist << std::endl;
            // Simulate playing audioData
        }

        std::map<std::string, std::string> getMetadata() const override {
            return {{"Title", title}, {"Artist", artist}, {"Type", "Audio"}};
        }
        ~AudioFile() { std::cout << "AudioFile destructor.\n"; }
    };

    // Concrete class: VideoFile (Playable, MetadataProvider, Editable)
    class VideoFile : public IPlayable, public IMetadataProvider, public IEditable {
    private:
        std::string title;
        int durationSeconds;
        std::string videoContent;
    public:
        VideoFile(const std::string& t, int d, const std::string& content)
            : title(t), durationSeconds(d), videoContent(content) {}

        void play() override {
            std::cout << "Playing video: " << title << " (" << durationSeconds << "s)" << std::endl;
            // Simulate playing videoContent
        }

        std::map<std::string, std::string> getMetadata() const override {
            return {{"Title", title}, {"Duration", std::to_string(durationSeconds) + "s"}, {"Type", "Video"}};
        }

        void edit(const std::string& newContent) override {
            videoContent = newContent;
            std::cout << "Video '" << title << "' content updated." << std::endl;
        }
        ~VideoFile() { std::cout << "VideoFile destructor.\n"; }
    };

    // In main, you would create instances and use them polymorphically
    // e.g., std::vector<IPlayable*> mediaCollection;
    // mediaCollection.push_back(new AudioFile(...));
    // mediaCollection.push_back(new VideoFile(...));
    // for (auto& media : mediaCollection) media->play();
    ```
    This design leverages multiple inheritance to combine orthogonal behaviors (playing, metadata, editing) into specific media types, while using abstract classes to define the contracts that ensure consistency across the system.
